title: Elastic Fallback Mediator & Slab Grace Proposal
content:
Status: draft
Owner: Elena R. Morales (product-dedicated)
Goal: define a lightweight, operator-friendly mechanism to reduce hard evictions and customer-visible errors during sudden demand spikes in Dedicated pools by combining a small fast-fallback fabric, soft slab grace periods, and a mediation layer that coordinates ephemeral reassignments.

Context / Problem
- We frequently see tenant-facing errors or aggressive preemptions when multiple tenants spike concurrently in a Dedicated pool.
- Current approaches center on strict eviction or immediate soft-throttles; both are blunt and either harm UX (errors) or waste confirmed reserved capacity (overprovisioning).
- Need better per-tenant smoothing for short, high-intensity bursts while preserving long-term isolation and contractual guarantees.

Success metrics
- Reduce customer-visible preemption/errors during multi-tenant microbursts by 60% in A/B test window.
- Keep SLA-breaches attributable to autoscale decisions under 1/month for any tenant.
- No more than 8% additional cost (GPU-hours) in steady-state across tested pools.

Principles
- Avoid changing billing guarantees for committed/reserved capacity (no hidden overcharging).
- Keep deterministic fallback ordering (reproducible audit trail).
- Prefer recoverable, low-latency mitigations over permanent migrations for short spikes.

Core idea (summary)
- Introduce an Elastic Fallback Mediator (EFM): a control plane component that monitors pool telemetry and authorizes short-lived, reversible reassignments of ephemeral slab capacity to handle spikes.
- Slab Grace: a timed soft window associated with each ephemeral assignment that allows temporary relaxed isolation for up to N seconds before either reinforcing isolation, committing a longer-term lease, or cleanly rolling back.
- Fallback options include: moving tenant traffic to a quantized/faster model variant, temporarily increasing batching per-shard with capped latency, or routing a small fraction of requests to a hosted fallback lane.

Design components
1) Elastic Fallback Mediator (EFM)
   - Inputs: per-tenant request rate, p50/p95/p99 latency per route, current KV cache hit rates, available ephemeral slab pool, tenant commitment tier.
   - Policy engine: prioritizes non-committed tenants for reassignments but allows limited, auditable grace for higher-tier tenants when it reduces global failures.
   - Decision outputs: ephemeral slab assign, degrade-to-variant, route-shed-percentage, rollback timer.

2) Slab Grace Window
   - Default: 45s grace window for ephemeral reassignment. Configurable by pool and tenant.
   - Behaviour: during window, monitoring looks for tail-latency regression; if metrics stable, EFM may either extend or convert to a committed loan (longer lease) based on policy thresholds.

3) Degrade Variants & Fallback Lanes
   - Variant registry: small family of verified model variants (quantized, narrower context) per major model in pool.
   - Hosted fallback: small-capacity hosted lane for best-effort responses (lower throughput guarantees) used only when tenant consents or as emergency route.

Autoscaling interactions
- When autoscaler triggers node addition, EFM prefers to attempt local mitigation first (Slab Grace + variant degrade) for spikes < T1 seconds to avoid unnecessary ramp-up.
- For sustained demand beyond T2, EFM signals autoscaler with priority hints (which tenants are suffering and which lanes to preferentially scale).
- Autoscaler and EFM share a minimal priority contract: EFM may request a soft prewarm for specific model variants (short-lived) to speed recovery.

Burst options (operator-configurable)
- Soft Loan: lend ephemeral slab capacity to tenant A for short window; loan tracked in ledger, used to reconcile billing/credits later.
- Variant Shift: shift a percentage of requests to model-quantized variant with smaller GPU footprint and bounded quality delta.
- Split-Route: probabilistically send 10-20% of requests to hosted fallback to keep tail under control.
- Graceful Shed: controlled rate-limiting with priority-based queuing for low-priority routes.

Isolation controls and guardrails
- Maximum concurrent soft loans per pool (default: 3).
- Per-tenant daily soft loan cap (seconds of GPU-equivalent) mapped to commitment tier.
- Immediate audit log entry for any reassignment that affects a committed tenant; retention for 90 days.
- Auto-rollback thresholds: if p99 latency increases by >30% or error rate increases by >2ppt during grace window, rollback and trigger immediate fallback route.

Operator and product UX
- Console: add "EFM activity" timeline in Dedicated pool dashboard showing loans, grace windows, and rollback actions.
- Per-tenant: activity feed showing when fallback was used and approximate degraded-requests fraction (useful for customer success).
- API: allow tenants to opt-in for hosted fallback, or configure preferred degrade variants and acceptable quality delta.

Runbook (operator notes)
- Detect: autoscaler alerts + p99 spikes flagged by SLO watcher.
- Respond: EFM will attempt first soft loan with a 45s grace. If rollback occurs, EFM logs and notifies on-call with tags: efm.rollback.<pool>.<tenant>.
- Escalate: if repeated rollbacks for same tenant >3 in 1h, recommend manual commit or engage SEs for pattern analysis.

Telemetry / Metrics to collect
- Soft-loans-granted/sec (by pool, by tenant)
- Average grace-window duration and % extended -> helps tune default timers
- % requests served by degrade-variant vs primary
- p50/p95/p99 for primary vs degraded lane (track quality regression)
- Incidence of rollbacks and root cause labels (autoscale, variant-regression, infra)

Experiment plan (A/B)
- Phase A (pilot): enable EFM in two small Dedicated pools for 2 weeks; route only non-committed tenants. Measure error rate, preemptions, and marginal cost.
- Phase B: expand to mixed-tenure pools and allow one higher-tier soft loan per week. Evaluate customer-reported quality impact and ops overhead.

Open questions / TODOs
- Default grace-window length: 45s is a starting point; should we consider 20s for high-density pools?
- Billing model for soft loans: ledger + crediting vs explicit meter-based replay charge? Need finance input.
- Security/attack surface: could a tenant intentionally spike repeatedly to get preferential loans? Need fairness heuristics (cooldown windows).
- Implementation complexity: how tightly do we integrate EFM with current autoscaler? Minimum viable: EFM as independent controller with a small API contract.

Next steps
- Align with infra (SRE) and autoscale owners to map minimal data contract and telemetry events (owner: Samir).
- Build a small simulator to replay historical spike events and validate rollback thresholds (owner: Priya).
- Draft runbook snippets and Alerts for on-call (owner: Noah).
- Present pilot plan to product leadership by 2024-03-22.

Notes to self / rough ideas (working doc style)
- Could tie soft loan ledger credits into Dedicated billing UI so accounts see transparent 'loan usage' and request committed upgrade.
- Consider allowing tenant-side preferences for quality vs latency to choose which fallback variant we use.
- Slack thread: #dedicated-ops for pilot coordination (see pinned messages).

References and quick links
- Related tickets: JIRA-RD-3421 (pilot request), JIRA-OPS-2998 (autoscaler contract), CONFLUENCE-DEDICATED-345 (observability spec).
- GitHub: ops controller sketch: https://github.com/redwood-inference/ops/pull/678
